dispatch.note: What the dispatch DECLARES, read from the agent definition at the reviewed commit. A verdict receipt's modelRequested/effortRequested are validated against these values. This does NOT establish what the harness served, nor that the checkout the dispatch ran from carried this same definition -- both are stated gaps, not claims.

Direction: AI-Handbook issue #36 — Fable as a third set of eyes: technical review in the loop and plain-English counsel at every decision David makes blind. Phase 1 is the second of six increments (Phase 0 through Phase 5), and the phases run back to back. This increment makes true: **every Codex finding in a code loop is classified against the approved oracle and the threat model by a judge that reads only script-derived inputs, and the fleet can see, roughly, whether that classification changed anything.**
Product Intent: 1. **The record's evidence path has no retyping step in the normal case.** A tool result that came back inline is recovered byte-exact from the harness's own session transcript by a script, selected by the call's recorded input (PR, method, page, full page size). `agent-written` remains a class the record names for the case where no transcript is found. The same script recovers the adjudicator's own answer, so no judge output is retyped either. (Closes #75 for this container: the value is cost, not security.)

2. **B1, conformance triage, ships inside the existing `review-loop-adjudicator`.** For every finding in the record the judge returns one class — *in scope*, *out of threat model*, *out of product intent*, *test precision*, *misdirection* — with a citation into the record (an oracle section, the threat model, or the diff), or *unclassifiable: no oracle* where the loop has none. Advisory in rounds 1–2: the builder triages with the classification in hand and may differ, saying so on the thread. Binding from round 3: a finding classed out of threat model, out of product intent or misdirection ships as a recorded gap citing the class; a finding classed in scope, test precision or unclassifiable goes through the ordinary write-or-stop verdict under the `Worth:` rule, exactly as today. A decline on an out-of-scope class must cite the classification; no citation, no decline.

3. **The record carries what B1 needs and lacks today.** The threat model for every tier at the reviewed commit; the bugfix oracle's fields as sections for a `bugfix` provenance (today they validate and reach the judge as `sections: null`); a patch cap under which #73's 127,061-character diff arrives uncut. Finding bodies and the four plan-oracle sections already exist and stay.

4. **A gut-level measurement.** `/maintenance` reports, for the window, how many B1 dispatches ran and how many findings B1 classed out of scope. Both are counted from the committed verdict files, nothing is stored, and the number is a trend indicator for David's "is this earning its keep" conversation — never an audit. The zero-for-fifteen retirement rule reads that trend.

5. **A harness-side observation of instruction isolation on every `fable-dispatch` run**, recorded beside the probe's self-report: the harness's own prompt-token accounting, the largest across the run's assistant events, bounded against the payload the script sent plus an allowance; and the debug log's loaded-skills and pending-async-hooks lines under their real names. Measured 2026-09-11 on Claude Code 2.1.268 (Haiku, replaced system prompt, no tools): 804 prompt tokens under the dispatch configuration from the repo root, 874 from outside the repo, 17,810 with default setting sources from the repo root — the repository instructions arriving despite the replaced system prompt. Stated as observed within a bound, never as "proven absent"; the managed-hook gap narrows and does not close.

6. **The three standing #73 gaps close**: the permitted-role set is a predicate (a role may dispatch iff its brief is script-generated), not a parameter; `briefSha256` hashes the text the reviewer was actually sent; a `result` event carrying neither `subtype` nor `is_error` is refused.

7. **No model id is hard-coded anywhere the machinery chooses a model** (David, 2026-09-11: "Fable" and "Astra" mean *the strongest Claude model* and *the strongest Codex or ChatGPT model*, not a version). Role definitions and the plan reviewer name a tier; one configuration value per tier, in `.agents/machinery.json`, maps it to the current full id; the dispatch resolves the tier there, records the resolved id and the model the answer was actually stamped with, and refuses when they differ. A new model is a one-value edit. The adjudicator's `model: best` already resolves in the harness and stays as it is.
Must Not Change: - Codex's full fix-or-decline force on product code. B1 never vetoes a finding; every decline still carries `Class:` / `Worth:` / `Oracle:` / `Result:`.

- The adjudicator stays an `Agent`-tool subagent declaring `model: best` and `effort: xhigh`, dispatched with no per-invocation model; it is not migrated onto `fable-dispatch.mjs`. Its receipt validation in `review-budget.mjs` is unchanged: B1's output is not a receipt.
- The write-gate rule and its two invariants; the round-3-onward *verdict* dispatch; the leash and David-gate arithmetic; the tier budgets.
- `plan-review.mjs` and the plan loop: untouched, except that its reviewer model and effort pin read from the same configuration value as Product Intent 7 instead of a literal in the script.

- The dispatch transport (a subprocess, argv built by the script); role definitions under `.agents/fable-roles/`; never `--bare`. Every role except the probe stays refused in this increment; the refusal lifts in Phase 2 with the first role whose brief is a script-derived record.
- The never-list: no second Codex, no veto over Codex, no builder in-loop prose in any judge's input. The record's finding bodies are root comments only, replies excluded — true today, true after.
- The `Worth:` triage rule and the producer-scoped threat model: fleet contract as of 2026-09-10, applied here and not re-derived.
Settled Decisions: 1. **B1 is the adjudicator, extended** — one dispatch per round, on the record it already reads. A `fable-dispatch` B1 would be the migration decided *next* on 2026-09-10; that stays next.

2. **One plan, one implementation PR, sequenced inside it** (David, 2026-09-11). The capture path lands first because it makes every later round cheaper. Round 0's SC3 (split the dispatch-side work) is declined on that instruction.

3. **"Widen the record" is a delta, not a rebuild.** Bodies, the four oracle sections and the internal-tier threat-model note have been in the record since `68222ab` (#38, 2026-09-06); the delta is Product Intent 3.

4. **The isolation observation is the harness's usage report and debug log, not the reviewer's answer.** The self-report canary stays, labelled as such. The bound is calibrated in the implementation against the live probe and the saved contaminated control.
5. **The `worth` role candidate (#36 comment, 2026-09-10) is subsumed at round 3+** by B1's binding per-finding classification; no separate role.

6. **Threat model**: the builder's own mistakes, scoped by producer — and (David, 2026-09-11) **a mistake whose outcome is inconsequential is not guarded against.** Applied to this plan: no digest binding of the judge's answer to its record, no outcome lifecycle, no per-request token deltas, no advisory-on-retyped-evidence rule, no coverage refusals. The record's `provenance` block keeps saying which class each capture is, and that is the whole of the honesty owed.

7. **Round accounting is a gut-level trend, not an audit** (David, 2026-09-11). The two B1 numbers in Product Intent 4 are the whole measurement. Nothing anchors an outcome to a later pass, nothing supersedes a regenerated dispatch, nothing distinguishes a handoff from a stop.

8. **This steer is contract, persisted in this PR**: `claude-core.md` rule 5 gains the consequence bar in David's words, and the Codex-facing threat model in `agents-core.md` says the same thing where Codex reads it — so the implementation loop can decline the class of finding this plan loop spent three rounds fixing.
9. **Transcript recovery and the committed verdict files are scope added during the loop**, kept because they remove work, not because they add guarantees.

10. **Affected-surface inventory, run 2026-09-11** and re-run against the final revision: the adjudicator cadence is stated in six payload files (`claude-core.md`, `review-loop-adjudicator.md`, `pr-watch`, `bugfix`, `model-routing`, `working-modes.md`) and asserted by `check-contract-consistency.mjs`'s retired-phrase table; the Phase 0 refusal in `fable-dispatch.mjs` (3 sites), `fable-dispatch.md` and its test. All updated.

# Agent instructions — portable core (all agents)
SYNCED FILE — do not edit in a consumer repo.
This file is the fleet-wide, cross-agent half of the routing constitution.
It is maintained in the AI-Handbook repo and vendored into every consumer
repo by the handbook sync. An edit made here in a consumer repo is
overwritten by the next sync; change the handbook instead.
Unlike CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md does not support eager file imports, so a
consumer's AGENTS.md LINKS here rather than importing. That matches how
AGENTS.md already works — it is a routing file whose job is to send an
agent to the right document — but it means this file must be readable
standalone, by an agent that arrived from a link with no other context.
Write it that way.
What belongs here: the cross-agent working agreement, planning and
implementation standards, technical priorities, engineering principles.
What belongs in the consumer's AGENTS.md: the product's context-reading
routes, its subsystem map, and its setup/verification/CI commands.
> **Who this is for.** Every AI agent working in a repo governed by the
> AI-Handbook — Codex, Claude Code, Replit, and whatever comes next. It tells
> you **how to behave and what is non-negotiable**, independent of which
> product you are working on. The repo's own `AGENTS.md` carries the product
> half: what this product is, where its truth lives, and how to build and
> test it. Read both.
> **One source of truth for all agents.** These rules are shared. Claude
> Code's `CLAUDE.md` holds only Claude-specific ceremony and defers here for
> every cross-agent principle. When a shared rule changes, it changes in the
> handbook — never as a forked copy in one agent's own file or private
> memory.
## Working agreement with David
David is the product owner. **Do not implement major changes from a non-trivial
plan until David has explicitly approved that plan.** An ambiguous nudge or another
agent's approval is not David's approval. Full working rules:
[`docs/ai-context/agent-working-rules.md`](../../docs/ai-context/agent-working-rules.md).
**Two working modes — the ceremony in force is always visible, never silent.**
Default is **feature mode** (plan → approval → full build → PR). **Bugfix
mode** is a lightweight fix-and-commit path. For Codex, David turns it on by
saying so (e.g. a prompt starting **"Bugfix mode:"**); absent an explicit
signal you are in feature mode. (Claude routes by request shape with an
announced, vetoable classification — see the mode-entry section of
working-modes.md.) Read
[`docs/ai-context/working-modes.md`](../../docs/ai-context/working-modes.md) for the full
contract of each and how to switch between them.
**End-of-feature documentation.** Follow
[`docs/ai-context/documentation-workflow.md`](../../docs/ai-context/documentation-workflow.md).
**The per-merge close-out judgement is retired (David, 2026-08-20)** — the
heavyweight harvest now runs **batched at `/maintenance`**, covering every
product feature merged since the last pass, or whenever David asks. What
close-out owes instead is cheap and unconditional: a **harvest-notes comment
on the feature's workstream issue** — decisions and why, alternatives
rejected, gotcha candidates — so the batched pass inherits the session's
context. Process PRs get no harvest. This is distinct from a one-off
"remember this" (immediate targeted persistence), which never waits for a
batch.
**Workstream tracking.** Every unit of work — feature, bugfix, doc harvest —
has a GitHub issue as its spine, tracked on a private Project board and kept
current via `stage:`/`waiting:`/`mode:` labels — with **two** exceptions.
*Sensitive/disclosure-carve-out work* never becomes a public issue and is a
private draft Project item instead. *David's Replit fast-lane tweaks* —
display-only UI changes he makes himself during UAT — carry no issue at all:
the retrospective sweep is their accountability rather than the Project board,
so no agent should demand one for a fast-lane commit retroactively (boundary
and sweep:
[`docs/ai-context/replit-environment.md`](../../docs/ai-context/replit-environment.md)).
What that sweep *finds* is ordinary work and gets an issue like anything
else. Read
[`docs/ai-context/workstream-tracking.md`](../../docs/ai-context/workstream-tracking.md)
before opening or reviewing a PR — it covers the label conventions and what
must never happen (e.g. `Closes #N` in a PR body, which would skip UAT).
When asked to **plan**:
1. Inspect the repo first.
2. Identify source-of-truth boundaries.
3. Call out product ambiguities (ask David; don't guess intent).
4. Propose a phased plan.
5. Include tests and migration/backfill handling where relevant.
When asked to **implement** (an approved plan):
1. Re-read the approved plan + relevant `docs/ai-context/` files.
2. Confirm the affected files.
3. Make the smallest coherent change.
4. Run relevant tests.
5. Summarize what changed, what was tested, and what remains risky.
## Technical priorities
Prefer, in order:
1. Runtime correctness.
2. Durable data and source-of-truth boundaries.
3. Repository fit.
4. Migration and backfill safety.
5. Security, validation, permissions, and auditability.
6. Admin UX clarity.
7. Tests and regression protection.
8. Simplicity and scope control.
9. Observability and debuggability.
## Important product principles
- **Human-moderated decisions must not be silently overwritten by AI reprocessing.**
- **Runtime behavior must match admin preview and debug surfaces.**
- **Avoid duplicate sources of truth.**
- **Do not patch only the latest example — solve the general mechanism.**
- **A check earns its place only when the value can differ from what you
intended — which requires something outside your control to have produced
it.** A harness report, a network response, a real user, another program's
output: observe those and refuse on disagreement. Everything a hand-run
script gets from its own operator's argv falls into one of two kinds, and
the rule differs:
- **Derivable** — the script already holds every input needed to compute
it (a receipt path from role and head). **Derive it; do not take it as
input at all.** A check whose two sides you both own carries no
independent information — it fails only when the code between them is
wrong, and that code is exactly as likely to be wrong as the check
(AI-Handbook #73: four review rounds on one flag, then the flag was
deleted).
- **A choice** — it encodes intent the script cannot know (`--role`,
`--timeout`, `sync --to <repo>`). Take it. A cheap check that it is
well-formed — non-empty, numeric where a number is expected, a path that
exists — is catching the operator's own mistake, which is exactly the
threat model, and stays. A defence against a *hostile* value of it — a
planted symlink, a traversal, a hard link the operator would have to
create on purpose — is not, and the response to such a finding is to
decline it, not to guard (AI-Handbook #7: eleven findings and no added
safety).
**Ask who produced the value, never which directory the file sits in.** A
script that parses a hook payload, a fetched document, a webhook body or
another program's output is reading something it does not control, however
local it looks — and where that script exists to *constrain* the producer,
its input is adversarial by construction and validating it is the entire
job. Getting this backwards disarms exactly the code that matters most.
**And a consequence nobody would feel is not a consequence** (David,
2026-09-11). Two classes follow, and findings in them are declined rather
than fixed: **accounting precision**, where a miscount changes no decision
— how many review rounds a loop ran is a gut-level trend, not an audit
history, so machinery making such a count exact is pure cost; and **an
agent's influence over its own tooling**, where the agent that runs a
script is the only actor who could subvert its inputs and could equally
just not run it. The controls against deliberate action are a human's
merge and the server-side ruleset. Neither class is fixed because the diff
would be small: each fix costs a review round, and the aggregate is never
weighed at the moment one is chosen.
- **Prefer database-backed config for tunable operational settings.**
- **Migrations must be idempotent and observable.**
- **Async work must show status** at two altitudes (per-item + aggregate) — see
[`docs/ai-context/async-ui-status.md`](../../docs/ai-context/async-ui-status.md).
- **Ship the surface with the behavior** (no dead UI, no invisible backend), and
**enforce every permission server-side.**
- Pre-launch: features ship **on-by-default, no rollout flags**; **no new external
vendors** without David's sign-off.
## Planning standard
For non-trivial implementation work, create or update a plan using
[`.agents/PLANS.md`](../PLANS.md). **Do not begin implementation until David
approves the plan.**
**Reviewing a plan (not code).** Plan review does not run on a pull request
(2026-09-09). A plan reaches you as a **file in the checkout you are running
in**, named in the instructions you are given, with its review oracle
alongside. Apply the
[plan-review contract](../../docs/ai-context/plan-review-contract.md): review
the markdown as an implementation *specification* against that oracle and
against the repo, return a **complete** assessment every round even when
nothing is critical, pick one status label (never approval language — only
David approves), and never implement anything.
**On a re-review, what you are handed is not the scope.** You get a fresh
context each round, with the previous rounds' findings as ids, titles and
dispositions only. Re-read the *whole* current plan and re-verify it against
the repo anyway, reconcile every one of those findings (Resolved / Still open /
Superseded, where "the wording changed" is never Resolved), attack from a lens
you haven't used yet, and report what you actually inspected — including the
searches you ran — plus what you could not verify and why. The contract's
*Re-reviews*, *Report what you verified* and *Output* sections are the
authority; this paragraph is a summary.

# The machinery's threat model is my own mistakes, not an adversary — a local script is not a security boundary
## What happened
Making the review-budget guard and the readiness gate portable meant
replacing two hardcoded literals — the repository's `owner/name` and the
list of required CI jobs — with configuration. That is a configuration
problem. It was treated as a security problem, and it grew into one.
Each round of review asked "what if the working tree is edited before this
read?", "what if a same-numbered PR from another repository supplies its
snapshot?", "what if the branch commits a weaker policy than `main`?" — and
each answer moved the read somewhere harder to reach: from the working tree
to the durable ref, from the durable ref to the base commit, from a config
value to the budget receipt beside it. By round ten there were three
different trust anchors for one identity, a classification file ranking
their trustworthiness, and Codex was correctly finding the gaps *between*
the anchors, which is a combinatorial space. Every finding was real under
its own premise. The premise was wrong.
The premise was that the scripts must resist the person running them. In
this environment there is exactly one actor: the agent that edits the
working tree, commits to the branch, captures the snapshot, runs the gate
and posts the review request. Whatever it can "attack" it can also simply
not run. The controls that exist against deliberate action are outside the
scripts entirely — a human's merge click, and the server-side ruleset on
`main` — and no local hook can add to them, because the hook's operator is
the party being controlled.
## What worked instead
State the job plainly and design for it: **the identity checks catch
mistakes.** Declaring a budget in the wrong checkout. Capturing the wrong
PR's snapshot because every repository has a #7. Running a gate in a
consumer that still carries the seed placeholder. Those are the failures
that actually happen, and every one is caught by the same simple shape:
1. **One reader.** `.agents/machinery.json` is read from the working tree,
because it is configuration and that is where configuration lives. One
function reads it; it fails closed on absent, malformed, or placeholder.
2. **Stamp on mint, compare on consume.** Every artifact the machinery
writes carries `repo` from that config. Every artifact it reads is
compared to it. A mismatch refuses with "minted for X, you are in Y."
3. **GitHub's word is compared to config too.** A snapshot naming another
repository is refused: you captured the wrong PR.
4. **No trust hierarchy.** Not "base commit beats durable ref beats working
tree." One source, compared everywhere. (Receipts are still read from
the durable ref — for *durability*, so a decision survives the container,
which is a different concern that predates this one.)
5. **The guard path reads no config**, for an operational reason, not a
trust one: an exception escaping the hook exits 1 and the tool call
proceeds. There, the budget receipt is the anchor.
A finding of the shape "an edit to the working tree could…" is declined by
pointing here. It is not a defect in a mistake-catcher that its operator can
disable it.
## Takeaway
Before hardening a check, name the actor it is hardening against. If the
answer is "the person who runs it," stop: you are designing a lock whose key
is on the same ring, and every layer you add is a place for two copies of
the same value to disagree. Ask instead what mistake the check catches, make
it catch that mistake in one obvious way, and put the real control — a
human's approval, a server-side rule — where a local script cannot reach it.

body: **<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Migrate model tiers into existing consumer configs**

Add a migration path before requiring `models` here. I checked `scripts/sync.mjs`: `machinery.template.json` is seeded only when `.agents/machinery.json` is absent, so existing consumers retain their older config without this block. After syncing, both `plan-review.mjs` and `fable-dispatch.mjs` therefore refuse every invocation at `modelTier()`, disabling review machinery across the existing fleet until each repository is manually repaired.

Validate the complete adjudicator response rather than accepting any object with a string `verdict`. If the model omits `conformance`, duplicates or drops a `threadId`, or returns an unsupported class, this branch writes the result as a committed verdict even though the new adjudicator contract says such output must refuse; from round 3 onward the builder can then act on an incomplete binding classification and silently leave findings unclassified. This is program-produced input, so the repository's producer-scoped threat model requires treating validation failures as in scope.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Match transcript calls to the configured repository**

Include the call's `owner` and `repo` when selecting a capture. In a session that also queries the same PR number in another repository, the later foreign call currently wins; an empty foreign collection carries no URLs for the downstream provenance checks to reject, so it can be assembled as a complete empty reviews/comments/threads collection for this repository and undercount the loop. The configured repository identity is already available to this script and should be derived rather than omitted.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Bound each prompt using only prior deliveries**

Track the bound at each assistant event using only material delivered before that event. `promptBound()` currently totals every later stream line before comparing the run's maximum prompt usage, so a large tool result or response emitted after an initially contaminated assistant request retroactively widens that request's allowance. For example, a 10,000-token first prompt followed by a 30,000-character tool result passes the current 13,555-token final bound even though it exceeded the 3,500-token bound when the request was made, allowing the new isolation receipt to report success for context the dispatch did not send.

Reconcile this new requirement with the same always-loaded section's later instruction at lines 415–418 that the verdict is “never a file.” The detailed `pr-watch` workflow now requires committing `<record>.verdict.json`, but an agent following this contradictory primary contract can instead keep only the context comment; readiness merely permits the verdict file and does not require it, so the PR can complete without the durable classification that this paragraph says later readers will use. [core/.agents/core/agents-core.mdL114-L114](https://github.com/TheAnswerManIsHere/AI-Handbook/blob/5e97f0f8fc384e0c6e8c653edfd1f6164351b5ef/core/.agents/core/agents-core.md#L114-L114)
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Apply the configured effort to Fable dispatches**

Use `contract.modelEffort` when launching the Claude subprocess. `roleContract()` now resolves and stores the tier's configured effort, and the template describes that value as the reasoning depth the tier runs at, but `buildArgv()` only consumes `contract.model`; the receipt also omits the resolved effort. Consequently changing `models.strongestClaude.effort` has no effect on any `fable-dispatch` run, which instead uses whatever effort the harness defaults to while configuration and tests claim the tier controls it.

Limit this migration to `.agents/machinery.json` rather than applying it to every JSON seed. `core/.claude/settings.template.json` is routed through this same branch, so an existing consumer that intentionally omitted a top-level `permissions`, `hooks`, `env`, or `model` key will have the template default silently restored on its next sync—for example enabling `bypassPermissions` or installing placeholder database configuration. Settings are consumer-owned configuration, so absent settings keys can represent deliberate choices rather than fields safe to backfill.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Validate evidence fields on every classification**

Require a non-empty `why` and the class-appropriate `citation` before writing the verdict. Fresh evidence in the current tree after the earlier review thread is that this validator now checks `threadId` and `class` only, although the adjudicator contract makes `citation` and `why` mandatory and permits an empty citation only for `in-scope`. From round 3 onward, an answer such as `{threadId, class: "out-of-threat-model"}` is therefore accepted as a binding reason to leave a finding unfixed despite containing none of the evidence that makes that classification usable.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Bound bugfix sections before later PR-body prose**

Stop the final extracted field at the end of the bugfix-oracle block rather than at `live.length`. In every declared Tier A/B body produced by `bugfix/SKILL.md`, `Blast radius` is the last recognized label and is followed by Verification, the checklist, and the rest of the PR description; Tier C has the same problem after `Migration ceremony checklist`. All of that later author-written prose is consequently stored inside `planOracle.sections` and handed to a judge whose input is supposed to contain the bugfix oracle rather than the builder's surrounding narrative, allowing unrelated arguments or verification text to influence conformance and write-or-stop decisions.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Keep early product findings subject to the worth test**

Replace “written for by default” with the worth-based early-round rule used by `claude-core.md` and `pr-watch`. As written, an agent following this product-loop contract must implement every round-1/2 finding, while the same paragraph later permits an all-declined round and the primary contract says to write only findings that pass `Worth:`. This revives the automatic-fix behavior the change says was retired and can create avoidable commits and mandatory review rounds throughout consumer repositories.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Dispatch B1 for early internal rounds too**

Apply this round-1 dispatch rule to the internal tier, not only inside the `Product loops` section. The still-operative internal instructions in `claude-core.md` lines 334–340 and `pr-watch/SKILL.md` lines 61–72 explicitly say there is no judge in rounds 1–2 and dispatch only at round 3, so internal changes will skip the newly required early conformance classifications and produce no verdict files for those rounds. Because scripts, skills, and agent contracts are internal-tier work, this leaves the new Phase 1 behavior disabled for most changes in this repository and its consumers.
